title: Drunk Leaders and a Tested Stone
overview: Isaiah warns the proud, drunken leaders of both Israel and Judah that their false sense of safety will collapse, and points instead to a foundation God himself is laying.

parts.label: Samaria's fading crown (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Ephraim is the northern kingdom of Israel, and its capital Samaria sat on a hill above rich valleys like a flower wreath on a partygoer's head. The powerful one God sends is usually taken to be Assyria, which swallowed Samaria around 722 BC as quickly as someone gulps an early ripe fig.

parts.label: A better crown (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: For the survivors among God's people, the LORD himself will be the crown that never fades. He will give fairness to judges and courage to soldiers defending the city gate.

parts.label: Leaders who mock (vv. 7-13)
parts.note: Judah's own priests and prophets are just as drunk, and they sneer that Isaiah talks to them like toddlers, using sing-song Hebrew sounds whose exact meaning scholars still debate. Isaiah replies that since they refused God's simple offer of rest, they will be taught by invaders speaking a foreign language, and the lesson they mocked will trip them up.

parts.label: A deal with death (vv. 14-19)
parts.note: Jerusalem's rulers trust a deal, probably a political alliance, to shield them from invasion, and Isaiah calls it a pact with death built on lies. God instead lays a tested cornerstone in Zion, measured by justice, while the coming flood sweeps their false shelter away; Christians later read this stone as pointing to Jesus.

parts.label: God's strange work (vv. 20-22)
parts.note: Their plans will be like a bed too short and a blanket too small, giving no real comfort. At Perazim and Gibeon God had fought for David against the Philistines, and now that same power turns against his own people, which Isaiah calls God's strange, alien work.

parts.label: The wise farmer (vv. 23-29)
parts.note: A farmer does not plow forever or crush delicate spices with heavy carts; he uses each tool for its purpose and stops when the job is done. Isaiah seems to mean that God's discipline is likewise measured and purposeful, not endless.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the cornerstone in verse 16 first meant something in Isaiah's own day, such as God's promise to Zion or its faithful remnant, with Jesus as a later fulfillment, or whether it points directly and only to Jesus.
think: What is something you once trusted to keep you safe that turned out to be less solid than it looked?
